methodological_rigor.justification: The study is a retrospective secondary analysis of a Phase 2 trial (NCT04380337) with only n=37 reference-standard annotations, which the authors appropriately acknowledge as a limitation. The semi-supervised design (Model 1 → pseudo-labels for 81 additional cases → Model 2) carries a subtle risk of information leakage because pseudo-labels are generated by a model trained on cases that then also appear in the 5-fold cross-validation test splits; the Methods state 'the same n=37 test cases for evaluation' were maintained, but how the pseudo-labeled 81 cases were partitioned relative to CV folds is not explicit. No power calculation is provided for the segmentation endpoint (the n=37 was sized for the parent trial's cCR endpoint). Statistical treatment is reasonable (paired t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank, BCa bootstrap 95% CIs with 10,000 resamples, honest discussion of discordant p-values), but no multiplicity correction is applied across multiple model/rater comparisons, and the radiomic clustering 'two groups aligned with cCR' is descriptive without a formal association test or correction for 416 features. Post-treatment Model 3 performance (DSC 0.175) and the near-collapse of inter-rater agreement (0.362) are reported transparently.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The study addresses a clinically important question — objective, reproducible MRI assessment of cCR to support watch-and-wait decisions in LARC — but the design is a small (n=37) single-center retrospective secondary analysis of trial MRIs with no external validation, consistent with Oxford LoE 4 (low-quality cohort / case series for diagnostic AI development). Endpoints are surrogate (DSC against a radiologist reference; hierarchical clustering concordance with cCR) rather than patient outcomes such as OS/PFS or organ preservation. Translational potential is plausible: an automated, reproducible segmentation + radiomics pipeline could standardize cCR assessment, but post-treatment Model 3 performed poorly (DSC 0.175), and radiomic cluster findings are hypothesis-generating. The relevance score of 3 reflects a credible but still speculative translational path requiring multi-center validation before practice impact.

reporting_quality.justification: TRIPOD is the most applicable standard because the work develops and internally validates deep-learning prediction/segmentation models, with STARD-like elements for diagnostic accuracy. The manuscript reports study design, cohort description, MRI protocol, nnU-Net framework, cross-validation, and effect sizes with CIs — satisfying several TRIPOD items — but is missing a formal participant flow diagram, explicit handling of missing data, calibration metrics, and separation of development vs. validation samples (test cases overlap with the training pool via 5-fold CV). Code and model weights are stated to be publicly deposited on a redacted GitHub repository, which supports reproducibility, but the imaging data are not stated to be publicly shared, and there is no mention of a container, DOI-pinned release, or external test set. Protocol pre-registration is cited only for the parent trial; no pre-specification of the segmentation/radiomic analyses is described.

novelty_literature.justification: The core contribution — applying nnU-Net with semi-supervised pseudo-labeling for rectal tumor MRI segmentation and coupling it to post-treatment ADC radiomics for cCR stratification — is a meaningful but incremental extension of well-established methods (nnU-Net, radiomics clustering) into rectal MRI, where annotated data are relatively scarce. The authors appropriately position prior radiomic work in breast, lung, and prostate cancers (refs 15–19) and acknowledge that rectal MRI segmentation has lagged. Novelty is tempered by the fact that pseudo-labeling and nnU-Net are standard techniques, several groups have already published rectal MRI segmentation and radiomics studies, and the authors' own prior workflow paper (ref 14) covers related ground. No new mechanism, architecture, or first-in-class claim is made.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well-organized and readable: the Introduction frames the TNT/cCR/watch-and-wait context clearly, Methods are sectioned logically (cohort, protocol, segmentation, pre-processing, radiomics, statistics), and Results map cleanly onto Tables 2–3 and Figures 4–5. The abstract is quantitatively grounded and honestly reports the poor post-treatment performance rather than overstating. Discussion is appropriately self-critical about pseudo-label circularity, modality-channel treatment, and T2W–ADC spatial mismatch. Minor issues: Equations 1–2 are referenced but not shown in the extracted text, Figure 5's caption mentions a correlation threshold (ρ ≤ 0.9) that differs from the Methods/Results (ρ ≤ 0.95), and some paragraphs in the Discussion repeat limitation points already made.

key_strengths: Transparent reporting of a negative/mixed finding: post-treatment Model 3 performed poorly (DSC 0.175) and inter-rater agreement also collapsed (0.362), with honest attribution to a shared imaging challenge
Appropriate statistical rigor for a small study: BCa bootstrap 95% CIs with 10,000 resamples, paired parametric and non-parametric tests, and explicit discussion of discordant p-values
Semi-supervised learning yielded a quantitatively meaningful gain (mean DSC +0.087, 97.3% of cases improved vs. radiologist) addressing the annotation-scarcity problem in rectal MRI
Code, hyperparameters, and model weights stated to be publicly available on GitHub, improving reproducibility posture
Thorough and self-critical limitations section addressing pseudo-label circularity, T2W–ADC spatial mismatch, equal-weight multi-modal input, and single-center generalizability
key_concerns: Very small reference-standard cohort (n=37, 9 cCR) with no external or multi-institutional validation; radiomic clustering is descriptive and not formally tested with correction over 416 features

Potential information leakage in the semi-supervised design: pseudo-labels for the 81 additional cases were generated by Model 1 trained on cases that also populate the 5-fold CV test folds; the Methods do not clearly delineate how the 81 cases were partitioned relative to CV splits
Post-treatment Model 3 is not clinically usable as reported (DSC 0.175), which undermines the stated goal of automating cCR assessment — the application that most needs automation
No TRIPOD-style participant flow, calibration, or held-out validation; pre-specification of segmentation/radiomic analyses is not described (sample size was powered for the parent trial endpoint)
Minor internal inconsistency between Methods (Spearman ρ ≤ 0.95) and Figure 5 caption (ρ ≤ 0.9) for radiomic redundancy filtering
Novelty is incremental — nnU-Net plus pseudo-labeling plus ADC radiomic clustering in rectal MRI extends but does not substantially advance published approaches
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a competently conducted but preliminary single-center proof-of-concept with small n, no external validation, and a key clinical use case (post-treatment segmentation) that still fails. Honest reporting and solid internal statistics support a Tier 3 (JIF ~4–9.9) venue with major revisions to clarify the CV/pseudo-label partitioning, correct the ρ threshold inconsistency, and formally test the radiomic cCR association.
